blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Ken Thompson's 1984 Turing Award Lecture as a masterclass in subtle, insidious security vulnerabilities. The paper builds from self-reproducing programs (quines) to show how a compiler can be subverted to inject trojan horses into other programs, including itself. Thompson demonstrates a 'double-blind' attack where a malicious compiler inserts a backdoor into the login command while also embedding a self-replicating mechanism to reinstall the backdoor in future compiler versions. The brilliance lies in the attack leaving no trace in source code—only the compiled binary carries the infection. Colyer emphasizes the paper's shocking 'oh *!$&#' moment, where the realization hits that trusting any part of the software stack (even the compiler) is perilous. The moral is stark: you cannot trust code you didn't create entirely yourself, and the attack surface extends to any program-handling tool (assemblers, loaders, microcode).

TURING AWARD LECTURE

Reflections on Trusting Trust
To what extent should one trust a statement that a program is free of Trojan
horses? Perhaps it is more important to trust the people who wrote the
software.

KEN THOMPSON

INTRODUCTION

figures.caption: Figure 3.2 shows a simple modification to the compiler that will deliberately miscompile source whenever a particular pattern is matched. If this were not deliberate, it would be called a compiler "bug." Since it is deliberate, it should be called a "Trojan horse."
